messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaelo was forty-three when the night fundamentally altered. He had been closing out a commercial kitchen in downtown Honolulu, stacking supply crates near the staff entrance when a supplier he trusted turned aggressive. The physical confrontation moved faster than his training could process; the concrete floor against his back, the sudden, inescapable violation of his boundaries, the cold steel of a shelving unit pressing into his ribs—it was not merely an attack, but a profound dismantling of his bodily autonomy. Two years later, at forty-five, Kaelo’s trauma account still arrives with unsettling clarity. When Kaelo attempts to recount the incident, Kaelo finds the words surface effortlessly, yet the chronology fractures entirely. Hours collapse into minutes, faces blur into shadows, and before Kaelo can anchor the exact sequence, Kaelo’s chest tightens and he forces the memory downward, leaving the narrative suspended just short of its center. The psychological shift settled heavily into Kaelo’s daily routines. Kaelo had previously defined himself through the disciplined architecture of culinary work: commanding a brigade, executing precise plating, and gathering his extended family for long aʻiʻai feasts. Now, standing at the prep station, Kaelo feels utterly no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. His knives feel alien in his grip, his voice fails to project when Kaelo attempts to direct line cooks, and the prospect of hosting his next family gathering fills him with a quiet, persistent dread. Worse is the sensation that clings to Kaelo’s skin no matter how many times Kaelo scrubs his hands or steps under the shower spray. Kaelo feels dirty or contaminated because of what happened, a mental film that makes him withdraw when a coworker brushes past his shoulder or when the kitchen ventilation drops and the humid air grows thick. Kaelo is certain that his life has been destroyed by the trauma; the marriage dissolved, his dedication to the craft curdled into resentment, and Kaelo can no longer imagine a future where he isn’t perpetually bracing for another collapse. These convictions began to actively dictate what Kaelo could and could not recall. Because Kaelo had come to believe he was fundamentally ruined and unclean, Kaelo’s cognition started to treat the traumatic event itself as proof of that ruin. When the kitchen doors swung shut behind him during a cold storage inventory, or when a colleague’s hand rested briefly on Kaelo’s forearm to pass a heavy pan, the appraisal that his life was destroyed immediately flared, and that certainty actively blocked Kaelo before he could fully recall the details of the assault. Over the following months, this pattern compounded into a rigid internal loop. Kaelo missed two kitchen promotions, stopped returning his daughter’s voicemails, and began leaving the line during peak service to escape the sensory overload. The negative appraisal kept the memory fragmented and inaccessible, and the inaccessible memory kept the appraisal sharp and unchallenged. Last month, the threshold finally broke during a quiet dinner service. A dropped chef’s knife clattered against the tile, and Kaelo froze, his breath shallowing, completely convinced he was back on that concrete floor. His executive chef pulled him aside and firmly advised him to seek professional intervention. Sitting in the intake room, Kaelo grips his coffee cup with both hands, his gaze fixed on the exit. Kaelo came here because the silence between Kaelo and his past has grown heavier than the noise of the pass, and because Kaelo is terrified that Kaelo will spend his remaining years scrubbing at a stain that only exists in his head. Kaelo hopes, more than anything, to remember the man he was before the violence without feeling like a stranger to himself.
